summary: Describes LSP stitching in GMPLS TE, combining several label switched paths into a single end-to-end path, where each piece belongs to only one end-to-end path. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Label switched paths are the labelled tunnels that carry traffic across an MPLS network. This RFC describes how to build one long path out of shorter segments that are joined together at a node, and how the nodes agree to do that using RSVP messages.

subtitle: Building one end-to-end label switched path out of separate segments.

tldr.problem: A traffic engineering path often has to cross parts of the network that cannot run the full end-to-end path themselves, such as legacy nodes or a domain boundary.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LSP stitching: separate label switched path segments are joined in the data plane at a stitching node, with RSVP extensions that let the nodes agree on the join and set up their label swaps.
tldr.outcome: The result is a single end-to-end path in both the control plane and the data plane, without the stitching node having to be configured with the pair of segments it joins.

today: RFC 5150 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the LSP hierarchy of RFC 4206 and the RSVP traffic engineering extensions of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

sections.title: What Stitching Is
sections.content:
A stitched Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching traffic engineering label switched path is built from a set of different label switched path segments that are connected together in the data plane in such a way that a single end-to-end path is realized in the data plane. This document defines the concept of stitching and details the control plane mechanisms and procedures, routing and signalling, that accomplish it. Where they apply, the similarities and differences between stitching and the LSP hierarchy of RFC 4206 are highlighted, and the signalling extensions that stitching needs are described.

It is possible to configure a node so that it switches traffic from one path, for which it is the egress, to another path, for which it is the ingress, without any signalling or routing extension at all, and with the operation completely transparent to other nodes. That gives stitching in the data plane, but it needs management intervention at the node where the stitching happens. With the mechanism in this document, the node performing the stitching does not have to be configured with the pair of segments it joins. Stitching as defined here also results in an end-to-end path in the control plane as well as in the data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: A long traffic engineering path is often made of several shorter segments, joined at a node. This RFC defines how the nodes agree to join them, using the same kind of messages they use for ordinary path setup, so that the result is one end-to-end path rather than a set of separate paths.

sections.title: How Stitching Differs from the LSP Hierarchy
sections.content:
The LSP hierarchy of RFC 4206 provides signalling and routing procedures so that a hierarchical path can be created. Such a path, created in one layer, can appear as a data link to paths in higher layers, so that one or more paths in a higher layer traverse it as a single hop. This is called nesting. A hierarchical path may also be managed and advertised as a traffic engineering link. When it is advertised in the same traffic engineering domain in which it was provisioned, it is a forwarding adjacency path and the nodes can form a forwarding adjacency over it, though there is usually no routing adjacency between its end points. RSVP signalling for path setup can occur between nodes that do not have a routing adjacency.

With stitching, a path segment is created between two nodes instead of a hierarchical path. A segment for stitching is the moral equivalent of a hierarchical path for nesting, but there is one difference: a segment created in one layer provides a data link to other paths in the same layer, not to paths in a higher layer. A segment may also be managed and advertised as a traffic engineering link, in the same domain or another one, though that is not required, and if it is advertised then other nodes can use it in path computation. While a hierarchical path advertised as a traffic engineering link has a forwarding adjacency between its end points, a segment advertised as one has none. In that respect a hierarchical path link resembles a basic traffic engineering link more closely than a segment link does.

The counting differs too. The hierarchy allows more than one path to be mapped to a hierarchical path: if LSP-AB is a hierarchical path between nodes A and B, several paths can be nested into it, each with its own label exchanged over that hop, and each may reserve bandwidth on it. With stitching, at most one path may be associated with a segment. If LSP-AB is a segment, at most one path can be stitched to it, the segment is dedicated to that path, no other path can be associated with it, and the whole bandwidth on it goes to that path. Several segments may still be bundled into one traffic engineering link, as hierarchical paths can be.
sections.plainLanguage: The LSP hierarchy lets several higher-layer paths share one lower-layer path. Stitching does the opposite: a segment belongs to exactly one end-to-end path and carries all of its bandwidth. The segment also stays in the same layer, so the path that uses it is not built on top of it in the way a nested path is.

sections.title: When a Segment Is Set Up and Why
sections.content:
A segment may be created either by administrative control, as a configuration trigger, or dynamically because of an incoming path request. The LSP hierarchy defines one possible trigger for dynamic creation by introducing the notion of path regions based on interface switching capabilities, and in that hierarchy a forwarding adjacency path may be created when an incoming path request crosses a region boundary. That trigger must not be used for creating a segment for stitching, because in stitching the switching capabilities of the previous hop and the next hop traffic engineering links have to be the same. Local policies configured on the node should therefore be used for dynamic creation of segments. Other triggers for both kinds of path include cases where an end-to-end path crosses domain boundaries or satisfies locally configured policies, as described in RFC 5151.

The procedures apply to nodes that need to associate an end-to-end path with another segment of the same switching type, where the hierarchy procedures do not apply. The example given is an end-to-end wavelength path that traverses a segment traffic engineering link that is also wavelength-switch capable: hierarchy is not possible there, so stitching may be the option. The procedures can also be used for inter-domain traffic engineering path signalling, to stitch an inter-domain end-to-end path to a local intra-domain segment.

Stitching may also be useful for bypassing legacy nodes that lack certain capabilities in the control plane or the data plane. One suggested use is to stitch a point-to-multipoint RSVP path to a segment between point-to-multipoint capable routers, so that the segment traverses legacy routers that cannot act as branch points and shields them from the point-to-multipoint control and data path. The document notes that such a configuration may reduce the attraction of RSVP point-to-multipoint and should be examined carefully before deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment can be put in place by hand or created when a path needs one. Stitching is for the cases where the ordinary hierarchy does not apply: the two ends must switch the same kind of traffic, the path may have to cross a domain boundary, and the network may contain older routers that cannot handle the full path.

sections.title: How the Segment Appears to the Routing System
sections.content:
A segment is created between two nodes and may pass through intermediate nodes. There is no forwarding adjacency between the end points of a segment traffic engineering link, so although in the traffic engineering topology the end points look adjacent, in the data plane they do not have an adjacency, and any data plane resource identifier between them is meaningless. The traffic that arrives at the head end of the segment is switched into the segment contiguously with a label swap, and no label is associated directly between the end nodes of the segment itself.

A segment may be treated and managed as a traffic engineering link, numbered or unnumbered, and for an unnumbered one the schemes for assigning and handling local and remote link identifiers in RFC 3477 should be used. Where appropriate, the traffic engineering information of a segment link may be flooded with IS-IS or OSPF traffic engineering extensions, using mechanisms similar to those for ordinary links. Advertising the segment is not a requirement for stitching. When it is advertised, the information exists in the traffic engineering database and can be used for path computation by other nodes in the domain, at the cost of adding to the size and complexity of the link-state database. If a segment is advertised in the same domain in which it was provisioned, there is no need for a routing adjacency between its end points; if it is advertised in a different domain, its end points should have a routing adjacency.

The traffic engineering parameters defined for a forwarding adjacency should be used for a segment link as well, and the switching capability of the segment link must equal the switching type of the underlying segment, because a segment provides a data link to other paths in the same layer and no hierarchy is possible. A segment must not admit more than one end-to-end path into it, and once a segment is allocated to a path the unreserved bandwidth should be set to zero so that no further path is admitted. Several segments between the same pair of nodes may be bundled into a single traffic engineering link, in which case each component segment may be allocated to at most one end-to-end path, the unreserved bandwidth of an allocated component should be set to zero, and the minimum and maximum path bandwidth of the link should be recalculated.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends of a segment look like neighbours to the routing system, but they are not, because there is no label shared between them. The traffic that arrives is switched into the segment with a label swap at the end that receives it. A segment may be advertised as a link, but it is optional, and it can only ever carry one end-to-end path.

sections.title: The Signalling Exchange
sections.content:
Stitching an end-to-end path to a segment is a two-step process: creating and preparing the segment for stitching by signalling the desire to stitch between the end points of the segment, and then stitching the end-to-end path to the segment.

A node that wants to create a segment for stitching must say so in the Path message for that segment, by setting a new bit in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object of RFC 4420. This bit, the LSP stitching desired bit, must not be modified by any other node in the network, and nodes other than the egress of the segment should ignore it. The purpose of signalling it is that the segment is not conceptually different from any other path, and saying so explicitly clarifies the data plane actions to be carried out when the segment is used by an end-to-end path. It also allows the egress of a packet segment to allocate a label as described below.

A segment can only be used for stitching if its egress is also ready to take part. To say so, the egress sets a new bit, the LSP segment stitching ready bit, in the Flags field of the Record Route object Attributes subobject of the Resv message. If the egress supports the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object and its Attributes Flags TLV and recognises the stitching desired bit but cannot support the requested stitching behaviour, it must send a PathErr message with the error code Routing Problem and the error value Stitching unsupported. If it does support the behaviour, it must allocate a non-NULL label for the segment in the corresponding Resv message and must set the stitching ready bit in the Record Route object Attributes subobject. If the egress supports the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object but does not recognise the TLV or the bit, it should simply ignore the request. The node requesting stitching must examine the Record Route Attributes flags for the egress of the segment and must not use the segment if the stitching ready bit is cleared.

For packet paths that use penultimate hop popping, where the egress distributes the implicit null label in the reservation, the egress of the segment should first check whether it is also the egress of the end-to-end path. If it is, and the path requires penultimate hop popping, the node must send a reservation trigger for the segment with a new label corresponding to the implicit or explicit null label. This causes no disruption, because the segment is not yet carrying traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The join happens in two messages. The node starting the segment says in its Path message that it wants the segment used for stitching, and the node at the far end answers in the reservation message with a bit saying it is ready. If the far end cannot do it, it sends back an error. The node starting the segment must check that bit before using the segment.

sections.title: Joining the Path to the Segment
sections.content:
When a node receives a request for an end-to-end path, it may create a segment dynamically or map the path to an existing one. The switching type in the generalized label request of the end-to-end path must equal the switching type of the segment, and the other constraints, such as the explicit path in the Explicit Route object, the bandwidth and local traffic engineering policies, must also be used when selecting or signalling a segment.

The node that receives the Path message for the end-to-end path must use the signalling procedures of RFC 4206 to send the Path message to the end point of the segment, and in that message it must identify the segment in the RSVP_HOP object. The egress node receiving that hop should be able to identify the segment link from the information signalled in it. A numbered segment link uses the addressing scheme of RFC 4206, an unnumbered one uses one of the schemes of RFC 3477 to exchange identifiers, and a bundled link uses the component link defined in RFC 4201.

For a bidirectional end-to-end path, an upstream label must be signalled in the Path message over the segment hop. Because there is no forwarding adjacency between the end points of the segment, any label exchanged between them has no significance, so the node may choose any value and the egress must ignore it. The same applies in the other direction: the egress signals a label in the Resv message for the path over the segment hop, any value will do, and the node stitching the path to the segment must ignore the label it receives. Instead, the egress sets up its data plane so that traffic arriving on the segment is switched onto the end-to-end path downstream, and the stitching node sets up its data plane so that traffic arriving on the end-to-end path is switched into the segment, in both directions if the path is bidirectional. At most one end-to-end path is associated with one segment, and if the segment's bandwidth is already allocated the ordinary rules of RSVP traffic engineering pre-emption apply.

An end-to-end path that traverses a segment should record an identifier for the segment link in the Record Route object for that hop, in both the Path and the Resv message, using the address subobject for a numbered link and the unnumbered interface identifier subobject for an unnumbered one. The intermediate links or nodes that the segment itself traverses should not be recorded in the Record Route object of the end-to-end path.
sections.plainLanguage: The stitching node passes the path message on to the far end of the segment, naming the segment in it. The label exchanged over that hop means nothing, because the two ends of the segment do not share a label, so both ends ignore it and set up their own label swaps instead. The far end also records the segment, not the links inside it, in the path's record route.

sections.title: Tearing the Paths Down
sections.content:
Tearing down a segment follows the standard procedures of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, with or without setting the administrative status, and may be started by the ingress, the egress or any other node along the segment. The teardown of a segment should be treated as a failure event for the end-to-end path that uses it, and the matching teardown or recovery procedures should be triggered for that path. When the segment is torn down for maintenance, the ingress may treat it as equivalent to shutting down a traffic engineering link along the path and notify the ingress of the path, though the signalling for that event is outside the scope of the document.

Tearing down the end-to-end path follows the same standard procedures, but the teardown of the end-to-end path and of the segment are independent of each other, so one may be torn down gracefully with administrative status while the other is torn down without it. When the teardown starts at the head end and a PathTear reaches the stitching node, that message, like a Path message, must be IP routed to the egress of the segment, with the destination address set to the address of the segment's end node. Router Alert must be off and the RSVP time to live check must be disabled on the receiving node. The PathTear deletes the RSVP state for the end-to-end path and frees the label allocations and bandwidth reservations on the segment, and the unreserved bandwidth on the segment link should be readjusted. A teardown started at the tail end, with a ResvTear or a PathErr carrying state removal, must be propagated upstream by the egress of the segment, using IP addressing to reach the ingress of the segment.

If the segment was provisioned statically, tearing down the end-to-end path may leave the segment in place. If the segment was created dynamically for the path, local policy may tear it down once no end-to-end path is using it, and the document recommends a delay before that teardown so that several RSVP errors and teardown messages are not produced at once. The recommended interval is 30 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: When a segment goes away, the path that used it has to be torn down or recovered, and when the path goes away the segment may or may not go with it. The messages for the path are sent to the far end of the segment, using the address of that node rather than the usual session address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
From a security point of view the changes in this document model the changes made by RFC 4206: the control interface over which RSVP messages travel need not be the data interface that the message names for switching traffic. That capability was introduced in RFC 3473 to support out-of-fiber control channels, so there is nothing new in the concept for signalling or security.

Using the facility means that the sending or receiving interface may change as routing changes, so those interfaces cannot be used to establish security associations between neighbours, and security associations must be bound to the communicating neighbours themselves. RFC 2747 provides the solution: an IP address is a valid identifier for the sending interface, and since the RSVP messages for a path are sent to the address of the next or previous hop, every mention of the sending or receiving interface can be replaced by the receiver's or sender's IP address. That leaves the mechanisms of RFC 2747 usable unchanged for establishing security associations between control plane neighbours.

This document also allows the IP destination of Path and PathTear messages to be the address of the next hop node rather than the RSVP session destination address. That makes the IPsec Authentication Header applicable, which RFC 2747 had ruled out because the messages were encapsulated in IP packets addressed to the ultimate destination, and standard IPsec procedures can secure the message exchanges. An analysis of GMPLS security issues is in the MPLS security document referenced by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the control messages travel to a different address than the one the traffic uses, a security association cannot be tied to an interface. It has to be tied to the neighbour itself, using the neighbour's IP address as the identifier, which is what the RSVP security document allows. The change also makes ordinary IPsec usable for these messages.
